text: The American Dialect Society (ADS), established in 1889, is a learned society dedicated to the study of the English language in North America, and of other languages or dialects of other languages influencing it or influenced by it. The Society publishes the academic journal American Speech. Founded as part of an effort to create a comprehensive American dialect dictionary, the ADS was established in 1889 by a group of American philologists when Joseph Wright began editing the English Dialect Dictionary, with the goal of producing a similar work for the United States. Its original constitution from 1890 defined its objective as "the investigation of the spoken English of the United States and Canada," a mission that has remained essentially unchanged, only expanded in 1991 to include "the English language in North America, together with other languages or dialects of other languages influencing it or influenced by it." Members of the Society, which has never had more than a few hundred active members, include linguists, lexicographers, etymologists, grammarians, historians, researchers, writers, authors, editors, professors, university students, and independent scholars. The Society's activities include a mailing list that primarily focuses on American English but also covers other linguistic topics. Members began collecting material, much of which was published in the journal Dialect Notes, but significant progress toward compiling a nationwide dictionary was not made until Frederic G. Cassidy was appointed Chief Editor in 1963. The first volume of the Dictionary of American Regional English, covering the letters A-C, was published in 1985. The Society's other major project is the Linguistic Atlas of the United States and Canada. Since 1991, the ADS has designated one or more words or terms as the word of the year, with the New York Times noting that the Society "probably started" the "word-of-the-year ritual." The "Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache" (GfdS) has selected a word of the year since 1977. The Society also holds special votes each year to select words in various categories, such as "most original," "most unnecessary," "most outrageous," or "most likely to succeed." Several words chosen by the ADS appear on Merriam-Webster's Words of the Year lists.
